summary: Defines standard terminology and a taxonomy for web replication and caching, describing the pieces and protocols in use at the time. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Web sites can keep copies of content and use proxies to serve requests. RFC 3040 gives these components shared names and groups the ways they can select replicas, exchange data and work together.

questions: what is web replication and caching taxonomy
what is a surrogate in web caching
what is the difference between a proxy and a reverse proxy
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for web replicas, caches, proxies and their communication methods.

tldr.problem: Web replication and caching use many components and protocols, while people use the same terms for different things. Their relationships and communications can be difficult to describe consistently.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines terminology, maps relationships among clients, replicas, proxies and network elements, and surveys protocols used for selection, replication, configuration and cache communication.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3040 provides a reference taxonomy based on technology deployed at the time. It is Informational and includes some protocols still described as work in progress.

today: RFC 3040 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Web Caching Taxonomy
sections.content:
The Web grew beyond a simple client-server arrangement as operators addressed scaling needs. Replication and caching became two important infrastructure approaches, and some systems need both.

RFC 3040 establishes terminology and a taxonomy for the infrastructure and protocols described as deployed at the time. Some entries refer to white papers or work-in-progress documents to show technology that existed or was being tested.
sections.plainLanguage: Web systems use many kinds of copies and helpers. This memo gives people a shared map for talking about them.

sections.title: Proxies, Surrogates and Caches
sections.content:
A proxy makes requests on behalf of clients. A cache stores responses for later equivalent requests. A surrogate is a gateway acting for one or more origin servers, often answering from an internal cache; the memo says devices called reverse proxies are more properly called surrogates.

The memo distinguishes an HTTP-transparent proxy, which does not change messages beyond authentication and identification, from an interception proxy. An interception proxy receives traffic redirected by a network element, often without user-agent configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: A cache keeps copies. A proxy makes requests for clients. A surrogate acts for an origin server, while an interception proxy receives traffic redirected by the network.

sections.title: How Replicas and Proxies Relate
sections.content:
A client may contact a master origin server or a replica origin server. Replicas receive data from a master or other replicas. A client may also use local proxies or surrogates that answer as if they were origin servers.

Caching proxies can form loosely coupled meshes of peers and parents, or tightly coupled arrays that act as one service and divide the resource name space. A network element may intercept requests and redirect them to a proxy in an array.
sections.plainLanguage: Copies can be selected for clients, and proxies can cooperate in groups. A network device can also redirect a request to a proxy without changing the user's settings.

sections.title: Protocols by Task
sections.content:
The memo groups protocols by the relationship they support. Replica selection can use links, HTTP redirects or DNS responses. Replicas may synchronize in batches, on demand or through a coordinated process. Clients can configure proxies manually or use mechanisms such as PAC and WPAD.

For cache communication, ICP uses UDP to ask peers whether they have a resource; HTCP includes HTTP header information; Cache Digests share summaries of cache contents; and CARP divides URL space across a proxy array. WCCP, NECP and SOCKS cover other interactions with network elements or firewalls.
sections.plainLanguage: Different protocols solve different tasks: choosing a copy, updating replicas, finding a proxy or checking whether another cache has an item.

sections.title: Trust and Privacy in the Cache Path
sections.content:
A proxy sits between a client and an origin server, so the client must trust it when it supplies cached content. A proxy can also see requests from many users, making its logs sensitive.

The memo identifies risks including denial of service at redirection points, replay through cached responses, and access to information that was previously visible only at the network level. End-to-end encryption can also make resources unavailable for caching.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy can see many requests and serve stored copies, so users and origin servers need to trust it. Its logs and cached information need protection.
